summary: Describes several ways for a Mobile Access Gateway in Proxy Mobile IPv6 to dynamically discover a Local Mobility Anchor, reducing the need for static configuration in large deployments. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone joins a big network, a helper needs to find the right office that handles its traffic. This describes ways to find it automatically instead of using a fixed list.

questions: how does a mobile access gateway find an lma
what is a local mobility anchor
subtitle: Ways for a Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateway to find the right mobility anchor automatically instead of by static configuration.

tldr.problem: In a large Proxy Mobile IPv6 network, a Mobile Access Gateway needs to know which Local Mobility Anchor serves each attaching device, and configuring that by hand does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five discovery approaches: get the LMA address or FQDN from AAA during network access authentication, or derive or receive an FQDN or address from lower layers, then resolve it with DNS where needed.
tldr.outcome: It recommends the AAA-based solutions, with FQDNs preferred over IP addresses, because they work the same across different access technologies.

today: RFC 6097 is an Informational RFC from February 2011. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Discover the LMA Dynamically
sections.content:
In Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213), a Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) acts on behalf of a Mobile Node (MN) that attaches to the network, and a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) holds the node's mobility session. Large deployments benefit if the MAG can find the LMA dynamically, which reduces static configuration in the MAG.

Other drivers named are LMA load balancing and picking an LMA by desired service (RFC 5149). The approaches covered are not every possible mechanism, only those thought to fit PMIPv6 most simply.

One requirement shapes all of them: when an MN hands over to a new MAG, the new MAG must use the same LMA as the old one, to keep the session continuous.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper at the door must know which office keeps a visitor's file. Looking it up automatically beats keeping a long handwritten list.

sections.title: AAA-Based Discovery
sections.content:
These solutions assume the MAG is connected to a PMIPv6-aware AAA (authentication, authorization and accounting) infrastructure, with the MAG also acting as a Network Access Server. The PMIPv6 parameters are fetched in parallel with the MN's network access authentication.

  • LMA address: once the MN is authenticated and authorized, the AAA server returns the LMA IP address, and the MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) for the MN.
  • LMA FQDN: the MAG gets a fully qualified domain name and resolves it with DNS. The name may be generic for the domain, resolving to one or more LMAs, or may resolve to exactly one LMA.

The two can be combined: the AAA server may return a generic FQDN at first attachment and the specific LMA address on later attachments. For that to work the chosen LMA address must be written back to the policy store, for example by the LMA through the AAA infrastructure after it receives the first PBU.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign-in desk tells the helper either the office's exact address or its name, and the helper looks the name up in a directory.

sections.title: Discovery Using Lower-Layer Data
sections.content:
Here the MAG uses information from layers below IP, such as radio access or an IKEv2 IPsec tunnel, to decide which LMA to contact.

  • From the MN identity: the MAG builds a generic LMA FQDN from preconfigured formatting rules, using an identity such as the IMSI or GUTI that identifies the operator, and resolves it with DNS.
  • Received directly: the lower layer carries an LMA FQDN or IP address. Examples are the IKEv2 IDr payload and the 3GPP Access Point Name Information Element.
  • From a service name: the MAG builds an FQDN from a service or network name the MN signals, such as an APN. The RFC gives ims.apn.epc.mnc015.mcc234.3gppnetwork.org as an example FQDN for an "ims" APN.

The formatting rules are usually agreed among operators in the same roaming consortium or by infrastructure vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper can also work out the office's name from clues in the visitor's ID card or the service they asked for, then look it up.

sections.title: Handover Considerations
sections.content:
When an MN moves to another MAG, all MAGs serving it should use the same LMA. This is trivial if the domain has only one LMA. If MAGs can transfer context (as in RFC 5949), the new MAG learns the LMA from the old one. Otherwise another way to deliver the current LMA information is needed.

Relying on DNS during handover is generally not a working solution with more than one LMA, unless DNS consistently returns the same LMA for a given MN. The MAG could synthesize an LMA-specific FQDN from the MN identity, or use the MN identity as input to an algorithm that always picks the same LMA from a pool, for example learned through an SRV query (RFC 2782).

After the first attachment, the LMA tells the policy store which LMA was chosen. On a later attachment the AAA server then hands that LMA to the new MAG, as in the AAA approach above.
sections.plainLanguage: When the visitor walks to a new door, the new helper must send them to the same office. So the sign-in desk remembers which one it was.

sections.title: Recommendation and Security
sections.content:
All the approaches need functionality or infrastructure beyond what base PMIPv6 requires. The lower-layer approaches depend on system-specific lower-layer capabilities that are generally out of the IETF's scope. The AAA-based approaches can be implemented in an access- and technology-agnostic way, so the RFC recommends them, and says FQDNs should be preferred over IP addresses, following Section 4, Paragraph 4.1 of RFC 1958.

On security, using DNS to find a mobility agent has risks described in RFC 5026, but they are largely mitigated here because the MAG, the LMA and the DNS server belong to the same PMIPv6 domain. Even if the MAG gets a bogus LMA address, harm is limited since the MAG and LMA should authenticate each other, and RFC 5213 specifies IKEv2 between them. If AAA brokers or proxies carry the information, the path relies on their security properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign-in desk method works the same everywhere, so it is the favorite. Helper and office also check each other's badges before talking.
